title: Squares, moves, dice and coins
allegory: A Markov decision process is a board game: squares, the moves allowed on each, dice that decide where you land using only your square and your move, coins you pick up, and coins that lose a little value for every turn you wait.
map: the moves allowed on each square
dice that look only at your square and your move
transitions T(s' | s, a): the Markov property
coins picked up as you move
coins lose value for each turn you wait
discount γ: a reward t steps away counts γᵗ

chapters.name: What is the game?
chapters.note: reward curve flat ... is the agent wrong, or my setup?

cap.1: Before teaching anything to play, say exactly what the game is. Otherwise, when the learner fails, you can't tell a bad learner from a bad game.
cap.2: Every RL algorithm in this chapter optimises inside the same formal object. Writing it down tells you what a correct answer looks like before you train anything.
cap.3: An MDP (S, A, T, R, γ) specifies the problem; policies, value functions and every algorithm from Q-learning to PPO are defined relative to it.

cap.1: Think of a board game: squares, the moves you may make, dice that decide where you land, and coins to collect. The dice care only about your square and move.
cap.2: States, actions, a transition rule and a reward. 'Markov' means the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the path that got you there.
cap.3: Markov property: P(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t, history) = T(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t). If the observation hides relevant history, the problem is not Markov in that observation.

cap.1: A square's worth is the coins you expect on the next move, plus the worth of where you land, shrunk a little because it is one turn later.
cap.2: The Bellman equation for a fixed policy: value = expected reward plus γ times expected next value. When the rules are known, you can solve it exactly.
cap.3: With π fixed it is linear: v = r + γPv, so v = (I - γP)⁻¹r (Howard, 1960). The inverse is guaranteed for γ below 1; at γ = 1 the system can be singular.

curves.label: left: 1 coin now, every other turn

cap.1: A toy: go left for 1 coin now and every other turn, or right for 2 coins, each one turn later. Which is better depends on how fast coins shrink.
cap.2: Left is worth 1/(1-γ²), right 2γ/(1-γ²). Below γ = 0.5 left wins; above it right wins. Same board, different discount, different best policy.
cap.3: The optimal policy is a property of the whole MDP, γ included. Solving a tiny case by hand, as [2.1] asks, gives ground truth to test an agent against.

chapters.name: When it isn't Markov
chapters.verdict: The rules must depend only on what the agent can see now.

cap.1: If the board hides something that matters, the game breaks the rule. One snapshot of a ball can't tell you whether it is rising or falling.
cap.2: Markov is a property of what the agent observes. If the observation leaves out something the future depends on, add it, for example by stacking recent frames.
cap.3: Partial observability breaks the Bellman recursion on raw observations. Remedies: augment the state (frame stacks, velocities) or give the policy memory.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Bandit: a board with one square
Q-learning and DQN: hidden dice, sampled
RLHF: tokens as moves, a judge's coins

cap.1: Every RL method you'll meet plays inside this frame. Training a chatbot from feedback is one too: the moves are words and the coins come from a judge.
cap.2: A bandit is an MDP with one state. SARSA, Q-learning and DQN solve MDPs when the rules are hidden and must be sampled. RLHF frames text generation as an MDP.
cap.3: Framing a behaviour as an MDP states exactly what is optimised; reward misspecification and reward hacking are claims about R, where steering by RL succeeds or fails.

coda.title: Left pays now, right pays later: find where the best choice flips

caption.1: Left pays its coins now and every other turn; right pays its coins one turn later. Slide your agent's patience and find where the best choice flips.
caption.2: The curves cross where L = R·γ. Raise the right-hand prize and even fairly impatient agents go right. Do this sum before training, so you know what 'right' looks like.
caption.3: V_L = L/(1-γ²), V_R = Rγ/(1-γ²), so the optimal policy switches at γ* = L/R. The blow-up as γ → 1 is why the tabular exercises keep γ below 1.

where_else: Multi-armed bandits: the MDP with a single state
SARSA, Q-learning and DQN: solving an MDP when the rules are hidden and must be sampled
RLHF: text generation as an MDP, with tokens as actions and a reward model's score at the end
Planning by search, as in MCTS, inside a known MDP

hamming.what: The formal game RL optimises inside: states, actions, transitions that depend only on the current state and action, rewards, and a discount.
hamming.when: Before writing any RL code: define the MDP, and solve a tiny one by hand so you know what right looks like.
hamming.why: Every algorithm from Q-learning to PPO and RLHF is defined relative to it, and many failures trace back to a mis-specified state, reward or discount.

object.title: The game board
object.subtitle: The whole now-or-later toy as a board: a home square and two side squares, with coins paid on the moves.

cap.1: The whole game on one board: a home square and two side squares. From home you choose left or right; from a side square you always walk home.
cap.2: Three states, two actions at home, one forced action elsewhere. Deterministic transitions.
cap.3: S = {home, left, right}; A(home) = {L, R}; T is deterministic, so the policy choice lives entirely at home.

cap.1: Left pays 1 coin on the way in. Right pays nothing going in, but 2 coins on the way back, one turn later.
cap.2: Rewards sit on moves: R(home, L) = 1, R(right, back) = 2, the rest 0.
cap.3: Reward timing is the whole contrast: equal cycle lengths, different delays.

cap.1: Here the dice are simple: every move lands where it says. In general they can scatter you, but they only ever look at your square and your move.
cap.2: Deterministic here; in general T(s' | s, a) is a distribution, conditioned only on the current state and action.
cap.3: The Markov property is what lets the Bellman equation recurse on states alone.

cap.1: Loop forever and add up the coins, shrinking each by γ per turn. Patient players, above γ = 0.5, should go right; impatient ones left.
cap.2: V_L = 1/(1-γ²), V_R = 2γ/(1-γ²): the optimal policy flips at γ = 0.5.
cap.3: Same S, A, T, R; the optimal policy still changes with γ, so γ is part of the problem, not a training detail.

predict.q: A multi-armed bandit is an MDP with how many states?
predict.why: With one state there are no transitions to learn, only which arm pays best.

predict.q: In the toy, γ = 0.9. Left or right?
predict.why: Right wins when 2γ > 1, i.e. γ > 0.5. At 0.9, right is worth 1.8 times left.

predict.q: Your observation is one video frame of a moving ball. Is it Markov?
predict.why: The next frame depends on speed and direction, which one frame cannot show; stacking frames restores it.

object.where: Any sequential decision under fixed rules: board games, robots, and a language model choosing tokens for a reward.
